title: Every Little Bit of Warming Matters
summary:
Countries are meeting in Turkey for COP31, the climate talks. Ten years ago, they agreed to try to keep warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Now, scientists say that goal is out of reach.

The planet is already almost 1.5 degrees warmer. Heat-trapping gases from fossil fuels are still rising, and most countries are not on track to switch to cleaner energy.

A United Nations study says the best case now is 1.7 or 1.8 degrees. On the same path, the world could be 2.8 degrees hotter by the end of the century.

That small difference matters a lot. Tim Lenton, a climate professor at the University of Exeter, says every fraction of a degree matters.

Corals show why. Heat turns them white, called bleaching, and can kill them. There have been four global bleaching events since the late 1990s, and scientists say a fifth may be happening now.

Before the 2023 to 2025 event, 44 percent of coral species were at risk of dying out. Past 2 degrees, 99 percent of corals would be lost.
why_it_matters: Even a tiny bit more heat can change the world you will grow up in, from the coral reefs you might one day see to the weather in your own town.

background_read: Countries from around the world meet at climate talks to talk about how to slow down the warming of our planet.
The planet is getting warmer because gases from burning fossil fuels trap heat, and that heat can harm living things like corals, which turn white and can die when the water gets too hot.
Even a tiny bit more warming can make a big difference, so countries are trying to find ways to use cleaner energy instead.
Article_Structure: WHO: Countries meeting at the climate talks, scientists, and Tim Lenton, a climate professor at the University of Exeter.
WHAT: The goal of keeping warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius is now out of reach, and scientists say every fraction of a degree matters because hotter seas bleach and kill corals.
WHERE: In Turkey, where countries are meeting for COP31, and in the world's oceans, where corals live.
WHY: Heat-trapping gases from fossil fuels are still rising, and most countries are not on track to switch to cleaner energy.
